questions.question: In the property-graph version of the Alice example, where is the fact "since 2019" stored?

options.text: As a property of the Person node for Alice
As a property of the WORKS_AT edge from Alice to Acme
As a fourth element of an RDF triple
On a separate Year node linked to Acme

questions.explanation: Lesson 42.1 stores the date on the edge itself, since an edge in a property graph can carry its own properties. An RDF triple has exactly three slots (subject, predicate, object), so it has no place for a fourth value without a workaround.

questions.question: In the Lesson 42.1 run on 25 hand-labelled candidates, the schema accepted 14 records. What were the precision of those 14 against the hand labels and the number of accepted false facts?

options.text: About 79% precision (11 of 14) and 3 false facts

questions.explanation: The output shows 11 correct records among the 14 accepted, so precision is 11/14, about 79%. The other 3 accepted records are false facts, labelled by hand. The lesson stresses that these figures describe the hand-built test set, not a real extractor.

questions.question: Take two triangles, {0,1,2} and {3,4,5}, joined by one bridge edge 2–3, so m = 7 edges. What is the modularity Q of the partition that keeps each triangle together?
questions.explanation: Each triangle has L_c = 3 internal edges and degree sum K_c = 7. So Q = 2(3/7 − (7/14)²) = 2(3/7 − 1/4) = 5/14 ≈ 0.3571. Lesson 42.2 gives 0.0 for one community and −0.1735 for six singletons, and 0.6118 is the Q that leidenalg reaches on a different graph.

questions.question: On the same two-triangle graph, what is Q for the partition {0,1,2,3} and {4,5}?
questions.explanation: For {0,1,2,3}: L = 4 and K = 2+2+3+3 = 10. For {4,5}: L = 1 and K = 2+2 = 4. So Q = (4/7 − (10/14)²) + (1/7 − (4/14)²) = 3/49 + 3/49 = 6/49 ≈ 0.1224, which is lower than 5/14. Lesson 42.2 uses this to show that cutting a triangle apart scores worse.

questions.question: In the six-node counterexample of Lesson 42.2, one greedy move raises Q from −0.0556 to −0.0139 and splits community 0. Why does a greedy method accept the move?

options.text: Q is rounded to four decimals, so the two values tie and the move is chosen at random
Q rises because the expected-edge penalty falls more than the internal-edge count does, and Q never checks whether a community stays connected
Louvain requires every move to keep community sizes even
The Leiden refinement step is switched on during local moving

questions.explanation: Lesson 42.2 writes Q as L/m minus the sum of K_c²/(4m²). After the move, internal edges drop from 4 to 3, but the degree penalty drops from 104/144 to 74/144, and the net effect raises Q. Modularity scores edges and degrees only, so a move that disconnects a community can still raise Q.

questions.question: What does Leiden's refinement step add over Louvain's local-moving phase?

options.text: It makes the number of communities equal to the number of connected components of the graph
It places every node in its own community
It guarantees that modularity Q is never negative
It merges nodes only inside each community and only into well-connected pieces, and Traag et al. (2019) prove that the communities it returns are connected

questions.explanation: Refinement restarts each community from singletons and merges nodes only within it, under a well-connected condition. That stops a community from splitting as Louvain's local moves can. Option a is wrong because community count and connected components are different things. Option c is wrong because Q is negative for singletons in the lesson's two-triangle example, −0.1735.

questions.question: In the seven-node toy graph of Lesson 42.3, the seeds are A and E, and the edges are A–B, A–D, E–F and B–C. The hop-first hybrid ranks the nodes A, E, B, F, D, C. At what budget does the hybrid first include C?
questions.explanation: C is the sixth node in the hybrid ranking, so it enters at budget 6. The vector-only ranking also puts G, which has no edges, above C, so the vector top-6 misses C.

questions.question: At budget 40 on the synthetic graph of Lesson 42.3, two-hop hybrid recovers 43.0% of gold nodes and vector search recovers 21.6%. By how many percentage points does the hybrid lead?
questions.explanation: The lead is 43.0 − 21.6 = 21.4 percentage points. The 30.2-point difference is between the hybrid on the structured graph and the random-graph control, which is a different comparison. The lesson's sampling check gives a 95% half-width of at most about 4.4 points for a proportion from 500 questions.
